checks.claim: Water pressure grows with depth, so a dam must be strongest at its base.
checks.why: Hydrostatic pressure equals density x g x depth, so the load is greatest at the bottom; dams are built thicker there to resist it.

sources.title: Why dams are thicker at the bottom

checks.claim: A gravity dam holds back water with its own weight.
checks.why: Britannica: a concrete or masonry dam proportioned to resist overturning and sliding by its own weight.

sources.title: Gravity dam: definition, components and types

checks.claim: A spillway lets flood water pass a dam safely instead of pouring over the top.
checks.why: ASDSO: a spillway safely conveys reservoir inflows over or around a dam to the drainage channel, protecting it from overtopping failure.

sources.title: Practical Engineering: How do spillways work

checks.claim: A stilling basin at the foot of a spillway slows the water so it does not scour the riverbed.
checks.why: Stilling basins dissipate the energy of fast spillway water (often with a hydraulic jump) so it re-enters the river slowly and does not erode the bed.

sources.title: ASDSO: Outlet erosion control structures (stilling basins)
